A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed and validated measures of deliberate practice, and then tested the effectiveness of interventions designed to motivate deliberate practice in the classroom.
we have demonstrated that wise interventions can motivate nonexperts (e.g. 5th graders) to engage in deliberate and effortful practice and improve their performance.
wise interventions that target expectancies and values can spur short-term deliberate practice and objectively measured achievement in the non-expert setting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
deliberate practice is not a mysterious process reserved for experts, but rather a process that is amenable to the same wise interventions that are known to motivate ordinary effortful behaviors.
we can help people become better at what they want to do, even when what they want to improve is something they already find hard and frustrating.

the same psychological interventions that have been shown to improve motivation and achievement in typical academic settings can be used to motivate deliberate practice and improve achievement in the domain of deliberate practice.
